pieces.content:
QuincyAgain

Hey Magoovians,

Does anyone remember seeing the episode where our man-in-common befriends a bowerbird? I would be grateful if anyone had a copy to share or just an idea about it. Someone told me 'it does not exist', but I saw it when I was a boy in circa 1956, I think. We had an Emerson. Emerson produces a lot of manganese. In the show, Magoo couldn’t work out what kind of bird his friend was. When it brought him a dried lilypad, he thought it was a dragonfly. When it brought him a sheaf of buckwheat, he thought it was a sparrow. When it brought him a piece of a cast-off buoy, he thought it was a seagull. (When he caught the red blur of the bowerbird’s crest, he became suspicious.)

Anyway, these gifts were of use to Magoo—I think he used the lilypad to shore up an umbrella—and the bird appreciated Magoo’s unpredictable movements, and the way he would back and front into the walls of his small room. I laughed at this setup of mutual support. He was stoutly tender, as depicted in his hands. The bird laid out the objects that it would offer into a plan with wings. Each had a distinct capacity for sound: some loud, some soft. In the plan, interpersonal use-cases would form around such levels. It brought a mirrorball for the left wing. It was the first time I had seen a mirrorball, and I wondered at it—even if only on TV and even though was drawn poorly.

Magoo saw in a blear the stupid plan that the bird was building—its plastic, limbs, eggshell, and drinking cups—and started to figure it was a social model. He tried to talk to his neighbour about it, but the neighbour told him 'it does not exist'. The gall!, addressed Magoo to the imaginary frame of the audience, before tripping on the sprocket of a motorcycle, which the bird had newly augured as a caravansary.

There followed a nauseous dream sequence where the social model of the passerine-type thing's nest came to be. The dream broke out of the cartoon format and was shot on film, though Magoo and encounters between people were rendered on cels above places. This part was not funny. After his dream, Magoo was certain that the plan was a 'fall-and-stir', after his dream. Eventually the bird moved on. Magoo starts to eat the objects.

GammaRho

[reply removed]

parent.content:
Two scapegoats bounded up underneath the footbridge. They locked horns. They ate food—seagrass and walnuts—from each other's mouths. They had tested and chewed through fences opportunistically and were now here. Their left eyes were foggy, like an old person's. The irises of these eyes bloomed. In lieu of any other type of routine, the food that they ate from each other's mouths helped to make their circulatory systems go.

Visitors on the footbridge looked down and could see parts of the scapegoats. The visitors would have liked to repurpose them, but it is tricky to get down where the scapegoats are. The visitors wore white jeans and carried big white plastic bags. The scapegoats were naked.

Each animal with a brain inherits and does work on a four-dimensional taxonomic tree of the available forms of animal and their features. Efforts are underway to externalise these via the use of a neural scanner, grid paper, and a series of printed images of available animals. While the animal—such as a scapegoat—has a circulatory system which is going, the taxonomic tree is oriented on polar coordinates. At the moment that this isn't so, an organisational downward wave rattles through the brain of the animal, restructuring the tree into a proper Cartesian setup. This is felt as a brief thinking-of-all-animals and their features.

pieces.content: In a hallway with the door open, a Honeywell T87 will attempt to equalise the temperature of the continuous (available) world. It sits between the mirror-dresser and the coat-hook which resembles two of four talons of a lived-in bird, like a Fiji or an Imitator goshawk. The Honeywell has the brain of a bird but no mouth or Nest. In this arrangement and when you’re cold you might catch sight of the consternation of yourself in the mirror-dresser when you run around the corner of the living room to adjust the temperature. At least. Or the top of your head or your apparently open mouth. What you can’t see is the outcasting belly of the change in the air as it flushes through a white flyscreen: the plastic or enamel white an extruded quatrefoil egg which flauntingly comes off in drying and which the Honeywell is doomed to face. If you could see the change in the air, it’d spill like the extra-amniotic puff of the wind in 1362. The thermostat is a lens perplexing the evidence of environmental warmth upside-down and inside-out and dreaming and as percussive as the feet of the continuous (available) world.

Yes art should be like a dream, she said. But
the kind of dream where you are doing chores or,
better, inventing a new way to keep things tidy.
And no idea is inlaid, all clouds have pants,
you and I are especially alike.
